transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-04-30 16:00 PDT
Duration: ~64 min
Attendees: Jordan (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), Alex (Optimize PM) -- Maya (Aperture), Ravi (Platform), Tess (Security), Omar (SRE)

[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick intro - I'm Jordan, AE on the Optimize side, with Priya our SE and Alex PM. How's the audio?
[00:10] Maya: Good here. Thanks for doing the simulation demo today.
[00:15] Priya: Cool. Agenda for today - we'll run a console-forward simulation of qprofile generation, show sample INT8 and FP8 runs, the latency/fidelity overlay in the console, and then go through a short runbook for rollback and alerts. We'll pause for questions as we go.
[00:30] Ravi: Sounds good. We're mostly curious about real-world regressions on our clinical prompts and what guardrails you provide.
[00:38] Alex: Great — we'll specifically surface the fidelity waterfall and the worst-case fallback logic. Also show the telemetry hooks for per-route SLAs.

--- Simulation start ---
[02:05] Priya: Alright I'm sharing screen, you should see the Optimize console. First step: we import the model variant (we used a 30B open model for this demo) and the sample prompt families. The console recommends two initial qprofiles: int8-perf and fp8-fidelity.
[02:35] Maya: Quick question - those qprofiles, are they full model quantization profiles or layerwise mixtures?
[02:42] Priya: They're mixed: base quantization with a few sensitive layers pinned to higher precision in fp8 mode. The console will show per-layer sensitivity during the sweep.
[03:10] Ravi: How do you measure sensitivity? Is it log-likelihood delta or a task-specific metric?
[03:18] Priya: We support both. For the demo we enabled a token-level perplexity delta and a downstream classifier recall test you can upload. The console overlays both metrics. Note that sometimes ASR in transcription makes names weird, for example the instrumentation is 'k-v cache' but transcriber shows 'k v cash' — ignore the typos.
[04:00] [Priya switches to benchmark tab]
[04:12] Priya: Here's a simulated latency distribution for int8-perf: median token latency drops by ~28% versus baseline fp16, p95 improves 35%. FP8-fidelity shows smaller latency wins but much lower QA drift on our test set.
[04:35] Omar: Do you simulate cold-cache behavior? Our services see a lot of short-lived sessions and prefix caching isn't always effective.
[04:42] Priya: Yes, we included cold start samples. In the console you can toggle 'prefix cache hit rate' to simulate worst-case. That changes the latency curves and the recommended qprofile.
[05:05] Maya: Can we see a concrete failure case? Like hallucination increase or classification drop when switching to int8?
[05:12] Priya: Sure — switching to int8-perf we saw a 3.6 point drop in classifier recall on the medical-entity set for the most sensitive prompt family, but on the chatbot family it was imperceptible. The console flags prompt families where the degradation crosses your configured threshold.
[06:00] Alex: Important note — Optimize's sampling isn't deterministic; we run multiple random seeds and show a confidence band. For decisioning we recommend rolling int8 behind a canary and gating with real-time telemetry.
[06:25] Ravi: About telemetry, what hooks do we need to implement? We use Prometheus + Datadog.
[06:33] Priya: We emit per-request breadcrumbs: model variant, qprofile id, sample id, token latency, and quality signals (if you attach your eval function). There's a Datadog exporter in the console; we can also send events to your S3 for batch analysis.
[07:05] Tess: On security: if data leaves the VPC for hosted runs, can you guarantee no PII persists? Also how does KMS work with private deployments?
[07:15] Jordan: For hosted, we have strict retention controls and optional field redaction. For Private (VPC) you get a customer-controlled control plane, and we integrate with your KMS/HSM for key wrapping. We'll share the SOC2 pack and our private deployment checklist.
[07:45] [10:00 mark - simulation moves to runbook]
[10:12] Priya: Moving to the runbook — this is where teams often get stuck. Step 1: baseline with fp16 and define per-route SLOs. Step 2: run Optimize's qprofile sweep with your prompt families and set a fidelity threshold e.g., max 2% drop in classifier recall or 5% increase in hallucination score.
[10:45] Priya: Step 3: staged rollout — console supports canary percentage, automatic rollback triggers (latency or quality). We also show a 'worst case rollback matrix' that precomputes the effect of composite failures.
[11:20] Maya: How aggressive are the automatic rollbacks? We prefer manual approval but want an emergency automatic fallback.
[11:28] Alex: You can set two-tier controls — advisory alerts and hard-rollback triggers. Hard triggers are based on an aggregated quality metric across the prompt families you uploaded. Advisory triggers just open a ticket in your tracker.
[12:00] Ravi: For the canary, does the system route by percentage or by route name? Our traffic is sharded by customer tenant ID.
[12:08] Priya: Both. You can route percent, or route by attribute (tenant ID, region, etc.). We'll demo tenant-based routing in a second.

[14:00] [Priya launches a tenant-routing example]
[14:12] Priya: Here we create a route rule that pins high-risk tenants to fp8-fidelity until they've passed a 3-day acceptance window. Lower-tier tenants get int8-perf by default.
[14:35] Omar: That's useful. Our compliance team will want tenant isolation logs.
[14:40] Priya: The console keeps immutable audit logs per request (token counts, model variant, qprofile id, decision reason). These can be forwarded to your SIEM.
[15:05] Tess: What's in the audit log exactly? Can it omit content but keep signal metrics?
[15:12] Jordan: Yes — you can redact content. Logs will still carry identifiers, hashes, and the quality signals. That way you can prove governance without retaining PII.

[18:30] [Latency vs Quality deep dive]
[18:38] Alex: Let's look at the overlay view: X-axis latency, Y-axis quality delta. Each qprofile run is a point, with error bars. Here's a quadrant map: top-left is high quality, low latency (ideal); bottom-right is low quality, high latency (worst). The console suggests Pareto frontier candidates.
[19:05] Maya: I see an odd point labeled 'int8-edge-2' that's showing low latency but big variance. What causes that?
[19:12] Priya: That was a mixed-precision run with a few sensitive attention layers quantized aggressively. The variance comes from prompt-length sensitivity; short prompts see big wins, but longer clinical narratives show instability.
[19:45] Ravi: Any guardrails for long sequences? Our transcripts can be long.
[19:50] Priya: Yes — you can flag sequences over N tokens to require a higher-precision fallback. There's a per-request header we inspect to decide whether to use prefix-cache or go to high-precision paths.

[24:00] [Demo of stress test and fallback]
[24:12] Priya: Running a stress test now — we simulate a spike in traffic and a cold-cache scenario. You'll see the 'graceful degradation' policy kick in: first fallback to a compatible fp8 variant, then to a heavier but less quantized model if latency SLOs are missed.
[24:40] Maya: Does fallback keep session coherence? For chat stateful apps it's important.
[24:48] Priya: We keep KV caches aligned across fallbacks so session tokens map correctly; there can be sequence-level differences but we try to preserve conversational state. Note: some transcribers might show 'kv cash' instead of 'kv cache' — again, ignore those transcription quirks in the notes.
[25:30] Omar: How do you measure fidelity regressions in production? We cannot run full evals per request.
[25:40] Alex: We sample at route-level using a small percentage of traffic to run eval functions in a parallel pipeline, compare outputs to baseline, and compute a rolling quality metric. If the rolling metric crosses threshold, the hard trigger fires.
[26:10] Priya: You can configure sample rate per tenant. For sensitive tenants you might sample 5% with stronger checks; for others 0.1%.

[31:00] [Customer-specific constraints]
[31:12] Maya: Our regulatory team requires that any quantization-induced degradation must be reversible and auditable. We need a documented rollback runbook.
[31:22] Priya: The console has a pre-built rollback playbook. It logs exact qprofile version, seed, and sample artifacts used for evaluation. You can reproduce the run locally with the Optimize CLI. We'll provide a guidemap.
[31:50] Tess: Also we need to ensure keys never leave our HSM for private deployment.
[31:56] Jordan: For Private installs we do not manage your HSM keys; we only wrap at rest with customer KMS. We'll send the private deployment security appendix.

[38:00] [Pricing and pilot discussion]
[38:12] Jordan: For a pilot we typically do a 6-week sandbox: includes Optimize console access, 100k tokens of hosted runs for benchmarking, and SE hours for two bench days. If you'd like dedicated capacity we can quote reserved GPU hours.
[38:35] Ravi: What's the expected cost delta between int8-perf and fp8-fidelity?
[38:42] Alex: On average int8 cuts per-token compute cost by ~35% vs fp16 and ~20% vs fp8 for some hardware, but that depends on kernel support and sequence lengths. Optimize will recommend quantization that maps to specific hardware kernels to maximize savings.
[39:10] Maya: We're also considering doing the pilot in our VPC.
[39:16] Jordan: That's fine — we support private deployments and can run Optimize control plane with a private link. We'll include the deployment options in the pricing worksheet.

[45:00] [Questions and confusion points — real speech quirks included]
[45:05] Ravi: I heard 'backoff rules' — is that the same as graceful degradation?
[45:10] Priya: Backoff rules are a specific policy set: e.g., if p95>50ms then move 10% of traffic to fallback; if quality delta>threshold then immediate rollback. Some of the transcriptions may show 'back off rules' which is the same thing.
[46:00] Maya: We saw earlier you referenced 'confidence band' and 'seed variance' — how do you pick the number of seeds?
[46:08] Alex: Default is 5 random seeds in the sweep. For high-sensitivity workloads we recommend 20 to get a tighter band. That increases cost but reduces false alarms.
[47:30] Omar: About model artifacts — how do we pin a version? We need immutability for audits.
[47:38] Priya: Models are versioned with content hashes and qprofile IDs. Console keeps immutable snapshots — you can export the snapshot and store it in your artifact repo.

[52:00] [Recap & next steps]
[52:05] Jordan: Quick recap — we showed the qprofile sweep, the latency/fidelity overlay, tenant routing, runbook and rollback playbook, plus telemetry and audit controls. Next actions: Priya will provision sandbox, Aperture sends prompts, Jordan will share pricing and security docs.
[52:30] Maya: Sounds great. One ask — can we get a pre-configured eval for our medical entity extraction?
[52:36] Priya: Yes — if you send the labels we can scaffold the eval and run it in the sandbox.
[52:50] Tess: Also we'll need the SOC2 and your private deployment HSM integration doc.
[52:56] Jordan: We'll attach that in the follow-up email.

[62:00] [Meeting close]
[62:05] Jordan: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the artifacts and the sandbox link.
[62:12] Maya: Thank you!
[62:15] Ravi: Appreciate it.
[62:20] Priya: Bye all.

Notes: transcription includes occasional mis-typed product names and 'kv cache' variants; speaker attribution occasionally simplified. Artifacts shared: Link: https://redwood.com/sandbox/aperture-demo (sandbox invite), Security pack: https://redwood.com/security/soc2.zip, Qprofile runbook: https://redwood.com/optimize/qprofile-runbook.pdf

End transcript.
